The player may stand or sit, hanging the gong vertically about half a foot above the ground and striking its edge with a bamboo or rattan beater. In wooden kulintang ensembles the kagul often takes over its part. Related instruments among the Tausug, Samal and Yakan are less used now, with the highest kulintang gong controlling the tempo instead; the Tagbanwa use it to hold the rhythm of a piece and to accompany songs.

Its range sits in the upper middle frequencies, so it stands out clearly in an ensemble. A stroke produces a fast attack and a well-defined tone, and the resonance is relatively short, which makes the gong especially good for marking the exact moments of a rhythm. Compared with other Philippine gongs, the babendil is sharper and quieter, and its resonance decays quickly rather than being thick and deep like a large gong. That character lets it divide phrases clearly inside a kulintang ensemble and gives the group a steady frame in time, like the pulse of the music.

The babendil is a single narrow-rimmed gong from the Philippines, about a foot in diameter, larger than the biggest kulintang gong and comparable to the agung or the gandingan. Its centre is a sunken boss, so it is usually struck on the rim or the outer edge with a bamboo beater or a length of rattan, giving a sharp metallic sound; in the Hornbostel–Sachs system it is therefore classed as a bell. The player may stand or sit, holding the gong vertically by the rim between thumb and four fingers, and strike the basic rhythm of the dabakan drum or the low agung. It serves mainly as the metronome of the Maguindanao kulintang ensemble, and by tradition both men and women may play it; the Tagbanwa also use it to keep the rhythm and to accompany songs.
演奏者可站立或坐下，將巴班迪爾鑼懸於離地約半英尺處。持鑼時須垂直、略向外傾，以拇: The player may stand or sit, and hangs the babendil about half a foot above the ground. Hold the gong vertically, tipped slightly outwards, gripping the rim between thumb and four fingers with the thumb parallel to the rim. To sound it, strike the rim or the edge with a bamboo beater or a length of rattan, which gives a sharp metallic note. Begin with the basic rhythm pattern, using the strokes of the dabakan drum or the low agung as a guide.
